glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.CZK: Czech koruna: the currency used in Czechia.
glossary.net loss: When a company spends more than it earns over a reporting period.
glossary.ROE: Return on Equity: a measure of how much profit a company earns compared with its owners’ stake.
glossary.EBITDA: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization: a way to compare company results before counting several costs.
glossary.IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an app that brings coding and other development tools together.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.CI/CD: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery or Deployment: ways to automatically check code changes and get software ready to release.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
glossary.parameters: Learned values inside a model that shape the answers it gives.
glossary.multimodal: Able to work with more than one kind of input, such as text and images.
glossary.agentic workflows: Tasks where an AI gathers information, uses tools, and completes a job across several steps.
glossary.neutrino: A tiny particle that is very hard to detect because it can pass through huge amounts of matter without hitting anything.
glossary.IceCube Neutrino Observatory: A neutrino detector that uses a cubic kilometer of ice and sensors to catch rare neutrino interactions.
glossary.borehole: A deep hole drilled into ice to place detectors.
glossary.optical detector: A light-sensing device; IceCube uses these to catch signs of neutrino interactions.
glossary.Cherenkov radiation: A faint blue glow that appears when certain particles travel through ice faster than light does in ice.
glossary.astrophysical origin: Coming from objects or events in space.
glossary.SQL: A language people use to ask a database for information.
glossary.rc: Release candidate: a near-finished version shared before the final release.
glossary.query planner: A part of a data tool that works out an efficient order for the steps needed to fetch or change data.
glossary.agentic AI: AI that can take steps toward a task instead of only answering a question.
glossary.zero-day flaw: A security hole that attackers can use before its maker has had a chance to fix it.
glossary.root access: Permission to control nearly everything on a device.
glossary.Full Disk Access: A Mac permission that lets an app reach files it would otherwise be blocked from opening.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.runtime: The software that runs a program while it is being used.
glossary.static site generator: A tool that turns website files into finished pages before a visitor opens them.
glossary.node:fs: Node’s file system API, used to work with files and folders.
glossary.adapter: A piece of software that lets one tool work with another.
glossary.feedback loop: The time between changing code and seeing whether it works.
glossary.image-based: A setup where the running program stays in memory and can be changed without restarting it.
glossary.debugger: A tool that pauses a program so you can see what it was doing when it stopped.
glossary.macro: A tool that lets programmers add language features or transform code before it runs.
glossary.domain language: A language with words and rules built for one particular kind of work.
glossary.ERP: Enterprise resource planning: software a company uses to handle parts of its day-to-day work.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.nREPL: A way to send code to a running Clojure program and see the results without restarting it.
glossary.borrow checker: The Rust tool that checks code won’t use a value after it’s gone or let it be changed unsafely.
glossary.ecological niche: The place a species fills in its surroundings, including what it uses to live.
glossary.biodiversity: The variety of living things in a place.
glossary.natural equilibrium: The idea that nature tends to settle into a stable balance.
glossary.El Nino: A recurring change in Pacific Ocean conditions that can affect weather around the world.
glossary.re-wild: Restore an area so wild plants and animals can live there again.
glossary.Erlang abstract forms: A structured form of Erlang code that the Erlang compiler can read directly.
glossary.intermediate representation: A middle format a compiler uses to pass code from one step to another.
glossary.transpiler: A compiler that turns a program into another human-readable format, such as source code.
glossary.AST: Abstract Syntax Tree: a tree-shaped version of a program that a computer can inspect and work through.
glossary.incremental compilation: Rebuilding only the parts of a program affected by changes, rather than starting over.
glossary.Zigbee: A low-power wireless system that lets smart-home devices talk to each other.
glossary.calibrated reference: A trusted measuring device used as a yardstick for checking another sensor's readings.
glossary.LQI: Link Quality Indicator: a number that gives a rough idea of how well a wireless device is connected.
glossary.IP65: A rating for a device that can keep out dust and handle water jets.
glossary.Matter: A smart-home standard that helps devices from different brands work together.
glossary.Thread: A low-power wireless network that smart-home devices can use to communicate.
glossary.vibecoding: Using AI to make software from requests instead of writing each line yourself.
glossary.scraper: A small program that automatically collects information from a website.
glossary.bookmarklet: A browser bookmark that runs a small tool on the page you’re viewing.
glossary.prediction market: A game where people make guesses about future events, and those guesses have a price.
glossary.SQLite: A small database that can be stored in a single file.
glossary.DevOps: The work of getting software released and keeping it running.
glossary.boilerplate: Repetitive starter code you need before getting to the interesting parts.
glossary.agentic engineering: Setting up and overseeing an AI that carries out software work for you.
glossary.Type II fun: An experience that’s hard while it’s happening but satisfying to look back on.
glossary.Chapter 7: A US bankruptcy process where a business closes and its assets are sold to repay debts.
glossary.Chapter 11: A US bankruptcy process that lets a business try to keep operating while it reorganizes its debts.
glossary.fuel surcharge: An extra charge on a shipping bill meant to cover changing fuel costs.
glossary.LTL: Less-than-truckload: shipping where one truck carries freight for multiple customers.
glossary.crate: A reusable package of Rust code that you can add to a project.
glossary.metadata: Information describing stored data, like table names or row counts, rather than the records themselves.
glossary.interface: The names and details other code can use from a crate, without needing its inner workings.
glossary.type-checking: Checking that code uses values and functions in ways Rust allows.
glossary.rustc: Rust's compiler, the program that turns Rust code into software.
glossary.cargo: The command-line tool used to check and build Rust projects.
glossary.impl Trait: Rust syntax that lets a function promise a kind of result without naming its exact kind.
glossary.Send/Sync: Rust labels for whether a value can safely move between threads or be shared across them.
glossary.async fn: A Rust function that can pause while waiting, letting the program work on something else in the meantime.
glossary.right of publicity: A legal protection against someone using your name or identity without permission.
glossary.scraped: Copied from websites, often automatically, to gather material for training AI.
glossary.JavaScript: A programming language; here, it lets an agent combine tool calls.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.Hyrum's Law: The idea that people will come to depend on any behavior they can observe, even if it was never promised.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.IANA: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority: the group that manages key parts of the internet's naming system.
glossary.ALPR: Automatic license plate recognition: technology that reads vehicle license plates from camera images.
glossary.transparency portals: Public pages where police agencies can share statistics about camera use, like vehicles scanned and police searches.
glossary.warrantless search: A police search carried out without getting a judge’s warrant first.
glossary.Fourth Amendment: The part of the US Constitution that protects people from unreasonable searches and seizures.
glossary.FOIA: Freedom of Information Act: a US law that lets people ask government agencies for records.
glossary.counterweights: Weights that balance the lamp so it stays where you move it.
glossary.mouth-blown glass: Glass shaped by blowing air into it while it is hot.
glossary.3D-printed: Made by a printer that builds an object up in layers from a design.
glossary.competitive programming: Solving programming puzzles under contest rules, often by finding a solution quickly.
glossary.algorithm: A set of steps used to solve a problem or make a decision.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.coding agents: Software that can take a request and carry out coding tasks, rather than just suggest text.
glossary.lidar: A way to measure the shape of the ground by sending out laser light and measuring what bounces back.
glossary.street graph: A map represented as connected streets and intersections so route-finding software can work out paths.
glossary.cumulative gain: The total of all the uphill parts of a route, rather than just the height difference between its ends.
glossary.DTM: Digital Terrain Model: elevation data aimed at showing the ground without counting buildings or trees.
glossary.grade: How steep a stretch of road is; a higher percentage means a steeper climb.
glossary.surreptitious recording: Recording someone without them knowing it's happening.
glossary.data fusion: Combining information from different sources into one picture.
glossary.GTK: GIMP Toolkit: a set of ready-made parts for building desktop app windows and controls.
glossary.Adwaita: A library of interface parts and styles that follows the GNOME project's design choices.
glossary.Elm Architecture: A way to organize an interactive app around its data, user messages, and rules for updating that data.
glossary.effect: A task the app carries out outside its main state update, such as saving the todo list to disk.
glossary.widget: A piece of an app's interface, such as a text field or a list row.
glossary.GHCi: A Haskell prompt where you can try out code and see what it does.
glossary.callback hell: A tangle of event-handling code that becomes hard to follow.
glossary.backprop: A way to train a neural network by tracing how changes inside it affect its final error.
glossary.zeroth-order method: A way to improve a model by trying changes and checking what helps, rather than calculating an exact direction to adjust it.
glossary.activation: A changing value inside a neural network as it processes an input.
glossary.population: The collection of separate trials used to estimate how a change affects training.
glossary.gradient: A signal that tells training which small changes are likely to make the model less wrong.
glossary.loss: A score for how wrong a model’s answer is; training tries to lower it.
glossary.Mixture-of-Experts: A model made of specialist parts that only uses some of them for each request.
glossary.agentic: Describes AI that chooses steps and acts toward a task, rather than only answering a question.
glossary.inference compute: The computing resources used when a trained model generates answers.
glossary.rollout: A run where an AI tries a task and its actions are recorded for training.
glossary.red-teaming: Deliberately testing a system for weaknesses before someone else finds them.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.proxy: A go-between that gets information from another website on someone else's behalf.
glossary.Etherpad: A public note-taking tool the Wikimedia Foundation hosts for the community.
glossary.Wikidata Query Service: A tool for asking questions about the information stored in Wikidata.
glossary.Aedes aegypti: A mosquito species that spreads dengue and yellow fever.
glossary.Wolbachia: A bacterium that can make mosquitoes less able to carry viruses; infected females pass it to their offspring.
glossary.sterile insect technique: A way to shrink an insect population by releasing males that mate with wild females but have no offspring.
glossary.Experimental Use Permit: Permission to test a product in field trials, but not to sell it.
glossary.biopesticide: A pest-control product that uses living things.
glossary.linker: A tool that joins a program’s compiled parts into a file a computer can run.
glossary.drop-in replacement: A new tool designed to take an old one’s place without users changing how they use it.
glossary.target architectures: The types of computer processors a program can be built to run on.
glossary.bounds-checked: Checked to stop a program from reading outside the memory it is allowed to use.
glossary.panic: Rust’s name for stopping a program when it hits a serious error.
glossary.Cargo: Rust’s tool for building Rust projects.
glossary.bootstrap linker: A linker used early in a build process to help build tools needed later.
glossary.segmentation fault: A crash caused when a program tries to use memory it is not allowed to access.
glossary.aetiology: The cause or origin of a disease.
glossary.endemic: A disease is endemic in a place when it is regularly found there.
glossary.pneumonic plague: A form of plague that affects the lungs and can spread between people through respiratory droplets.
glossary.TCC: Transparency, Consent, and Control: macOS's permission system, which asks before apps can reach protected things like the camera or files.
glossary.headless Mac: A Mac set up to run without a screen or keyboard attached, and controlled remotely.
glossary.SSH tunneling: Secure Shell tunneling: a way to reach a service through a protected remote connection instead of exposing its port directly to the internet.
glossary.point release: A smaller software update that comes after a main release, often used to add fixes.
glossary.walled garden: A service that keeps you within one company's products and limits what else you can use.
glossary.antiferromagnet: A material whose neighboring atomic magnets point opposite ways and cancel each other out.
glossary.Luttinger-compensated magnet: An antiferromagnet where opposite spins cancel overall, but the atoms' different surroundings let electrons of each spin sort by energy.
glossary.spintronics: Using the direction of electron spin to store or read information.
glossary.band gap: A range of energy that electrons in a material cannot occupy; it helps determine how the material carries electricity.
glossary.spin window: The slice of energy near the band gap where the available electron states all have the same spin.
glossary.density functional theory: A computer method for estimating how electrons behave in a material.
glossary.Markdown: A plain-text way to format notes with headings, lists, and code.
glossary.Unicode: A shared way to represent characters from writing systems around the world in files and software.
glossary.ASCII: American Standard Code for Information Interchange: an older character set for basic English letters, numbers, and punctuation.
glossary.character encoding: Rules that tell a computer which characters stored values stand for.
glossary.line ending: A marker that shows where one line of text stops and the next begins.
glossary.POSIX: Portable Operating System Interface: shared rules for how Unix-like systems behave.
glossary.Base64: A way to represent data as ordinary text characters, even when the data itself is not text.
glossary.command line: A way to use a computer by typing instructions instead of clicking through menus.
glossary.LogicFolding: A chip design that uses multiple wafer layers so signals can travel less distance between parts.
glossary.Entity List: A US government list of organizations that can face restrictions on US companies doing business with them.
glossary.SEP: Standard-Essential Patent: A patent covering something companies need to use to follow shared rules for how products work.
glossary.FRAND: Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory: A promise that patent licenses will be offered on fair terms.
glossary.cross-licensing: When two companies give each other permission to use patents.
